name: Radiation-proof probe memory
subtitle: a memory that outlives centuries of space radiation

effects.effect: tiny stable magnetic whirls can be pushed along a wire with very little current
a current of spin-aligned electrons can flip a tiny magnet
radiation from space grows stronger with altitude

effect: tiny stable magnetic whirls can be pushed along a wire with very little current
how: A probe sent to another star, or a vault left on the Moon, loses its memory long before it arrives: ordinary chips store each bit as a little pocket of charge, and a single cosmic ray flips it. A bit stored as a tiny magnetic whirl holds no charge for a ray to disturb, and the whirl is knotted in a way that cannot simply unwind, so it survives heat and radiation that erase anything else; a trickle of spin-aligned current walks the whirls along a wire to the reader.
obstacle: Whirls have only been driven reliably in laboratory strips, and they drift sideways as they move, which scrambles the order of the bits.
why: Charge-free bits remove the very mechanism by which space erases memory.
real: Skyrmion racetrack memory remains a proposal - reviews state a fully functional skyrmion racetrack memory has not been experimentally demonstrated, with edge annihilation and pinning unsolved - and no radiation-hardness testing of skyrmion storage was found; the charge-free radiation argument exists only for RRAM.
